title: Sticks Into a Square Frame
statement:
You get the lengths of some sticks in sticks. Can you build the outline of a square using every stick exactly once? Sticks may be joined end to end along a side, but never broken.

Return true if a square can be formed, otherwise false.

examples.why: The total is 16, so each side is 4: 3+1, 3+1, 2+2, 2+2.
The total 16 divides by 4 and no stick is longer than 4, yet each 3 would need a 1 to finish its side.

hints: Some checks are free: the total must divide by 4, and no stick can be longer than a side.
Place sticks one by one into one of four sides, never letting a side exceed the target. Which order of sticks makes dead ends show up early?
Sort sticks from longest to shortest. When placing a stick, skip a side whose current length equals one you already tried for this stick: the result would be a mirror image of a failed attempt.

explain.intuition:
Each side must be exactly total / 4. So the question is whether the sticks split into four groups with that sum. With at most 15 sticks, a search over assignments is fine, as long as it cuts off hopeless branches early.

Two prunings make it fast. Place the longest sticks first: a long stick has few places to go, so a bad partial choice fails within a few steps instead of after placing every small stick. And if two sides currently have the same length, putting the stick on either one leads to the same situations, so try only one of them. Without this, an empty square has four identical sides and the search repeats every failure four times over.
steps: Compute the total. If it does not divide by 4, return false. Let side = total / 4.
Sort the sticks in decreasing order. If the longest one is over side, return false.
Recurse over sticks by index, keeping four running side lengths. For stick i, try each side that has room for it and whose length differs from the sides already tried for this stick.
Add the stick, recurse on i + 1, and remove it again if that fails.
When every stick is placed, all four sides are full, so return true.
pitfalls: Trying every side for every stick without skipping sides of equal length. With 15 sticks and no answer, the search explores each arrangement up to 24 times (once per ordering of the sides) and runs out of time.
Forgetting the divisibility check. Without it, sides can never be exact and the search runs to exhaustion.
Only checking that the total divides by 4. [3, 3, 3, 3, 4] passes that test and still fails.

complexity.time: O(4^n) worst case, far less with pruning

solutions.title: Try every side for every stick
solutions.idea: Assign each stick to one of four sides in all 4^n ways and check that the four sums are equal.

solutions.title: Backtracking with pruning
solutions.idea: Longest sticks first, never overfill a side, and skip sides whose length was already tried for this stick.
solutions.time: O(4^n) worst case, fast in practice

solutions.title: Bitmask DP over used sticks
solutions.idea: For every subset of used sticks, the filled amount of the current side is total(subset) mod side. Mark which subsets are reachable, adding one stick at a time without overfilling.

followups: Split into k groups of equal sum instead of 4. Which pruning still applies?
If no square is possible, what is the largest square you can make using some of the sticks?
